usage: the default greeting to almost anyone you meet
반말, to a close friend, a child, or someone clearly younger
격식체; soldiers, announcers, staff to customers, formal speeches
natural extension when greeting someone you know
examples: A: 안녕하세요! / B: 네, 안녕하세요.
A: Hello! / B: Yes, hello.
the bare greeting returned with the same words — no extra 'how are you?' needed
안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다.
Hello, nice to meet you (first time).
everyday: chaining the greeting into a first introduction
(가게에 들어가며) 안녕하세요~ 사장님 계세요?
(walking into a shop) Hello~ is the owner in?
real situation: 안녕하세요 doubles as 'excuse me' to get attention in a shop
nuance: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose 존댓말 greeting for strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers — basically any adult you are not on 반말 terms with. The root 안녕(安寧) means 'peace/well-being', so the phrase literally asks 'are you at peace?', but modern Koreans hear it simply as 'hello'; it works morning, noon, and night since Korean has no separate 'good morning/afternoon/evening' equivalents. The register ladder runs: 안녕 (반말, close friends / children / clear juniors) → 안녕하세요 (standard polite) → 안녕하십니까 (격식체, formal broadcasts and service settings). A key social rule: saying 안녕 to a teacher, boss, or older stranger signals either extreme intimacy or disrespect — always default to 안녕하세요 until 반말 is mutually established. The classic English-speaker trap is splitting greetings by time of day or tacking on 어떻게 지내세요? every time — in Korean, 안녕하세요 alone is the complete, natural hello, and opening with a wellbeing question to a stranger sounds oddly probing.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'are you at peace?' (안녕安寧 + 하세요). In practice, Koreans hear it simply as 'hello' — the question about well-being has been bleached away through daily use.

Use 안녕하세요 as your default with any adult you are not on 반말 terms with: strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers. It works morning, noon, and night — Korean has no 'good morning / good evening' split. Do NOT say 안녕 to a senior or stranger; that is 반말 and reads as rude.
안녕 (반말, friends/kids/juniors) → 안녕하세요 (standard polite) → 안녕하십니까 (격식체, formal speeches, service staff). Chain into 안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다 for a first meeting, or 안녕하세요, 잘 지내셨어요? for a warm reconnection.

안녕하세요 is a neutral all-day greeting. 안녕하십니까 is stiffer and used in one-directional formal contexts (news anchors, soldiers, staff). 여보세요 is only for phone calls — never use it face-to-face as a hello.

English speakers split greetings by time of day (good morning / afternoon) and routinely add 'how are you?' — Korean does neither. 안녕하세요 alone is complete. Adding 어떻게 지내세요? to a new acquaintance sounds overly intimate.

mistakes: Saying 안녕 to a teacher, boss, or older stranger — that is 반말 and sounds rude/childish; use 안녕하세요 with anyone you owe respect.
Searching for a 'good morning / good evening' equivalent — Korean uses one 안녕하세요 all day; time-of-day greetings are not standard.
Writing or saying 안녕하새요 — the verb ending is 세요 (하 + 세요), never 새요.

english: Goodbye (said by the person who is leaving).
usage: YOU are leaving; they stay (in their home/shop/office)
반말, leaving a close friend who stays behind
격식체, e.g. leaving a formal office or addressing a superior
goodbye, keep up the good work
warm close to staff/coworkers who remain
examples: A: 안녕히 계세요. / B: 네, 안녕히 가세요.
A: Goodbye (I'm leaving). / B: Yes, goodbye (go well).
the leaver says 계세요, the stayer replies with 가세요 — the two phrases are a mirror pair
(사무실을 나가며) 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. 안녕히 계세요.
(leaving the office) I'll head off first. Goodbye.
everyday: pairs with 먼저 들어가겠습니다 ('I'll leave first') — a standard polite exit
(병원에서 나오며) 선생님, 감사합니다. 안녕히 계세요.
(leaving the clinic) Thank you, doctor. Goodbye.
real situation: patient leaving the doctor who stays — 계세요 because the doctor remains
nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the goodbye YOU say when you are the one leaving and the other person stays — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/stay', so you are literally wishing them 'stay in peace'. Its mirror twin is 안녕히 가세요 (가다 'to go'), said TO the person who is leaving; the verb encodes who is physically moving, and choosing wrong reverses the meaning entirely. Register ladder: 잘 있어 (반말, friend stays) → 안녕히 계세요 (polite) → 안녕히 계십시오 (격식체). In work settings it often pairs with 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work') for warmth. The number-one English-speaker error is treating 'goodbye' as one fixed phrase and misfiring 안녕히 가세요 as they themselves walk out the door — that literally tells the host to leave their own home.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please stay in peace' (안녕히 + 계시다 honorific of 있다 'to stay'). The phrase is specifically shaped for the speaker who is walking away.

Use 안녕히 계세요 ONLY when YOU are the one departing and the other person remains (in their home, shop, or office). Polite to any adult. Upgrade to 계십시오 in very stiff formal settings; downgrade to 잘 있어 with a close friend who stays.
These two phrases are a matched pair: 계세요 = I leave, you stay; 가세요 = you leave, I stay. Always ask: 'who is physically moving right now?' That person's verb is 가다.
잘 있어 (반말) → 안녕히 계세요 (polite) → 안녕히 계십시오 (격식체). Common warm extensions: 안녕히 계세요, 수고하세요 (to coworkers) or 안녕히 계세요, 또 오겠습니다 (to a host).

English has one 'goodbye' for all directions. Korean forces a choice based on who walks. The most common learner error: saying 안녕히 가세요 while walking out the door yourself — that orders the person staying to leave.

mistakes: Using 안녕히 가세요 when YOU are leaving — that tells the person staying to 'go'; if you exit and they remain, say 안녕히 계세요.
Saying 안녕히 계세요 to BOTH people in a two-way parting — only the person leaving says it; the stayer replies with 안녕히 가세요.
Spelling it 안녕히 게세요 — the verb is 계시다, so it is 계세요, not 게세요.

usage: 반말, to a close friend or junior who is leaving
격식체; shop/airline/hotel staff to a departing guest
examples: A: 안녕히 가세요. / B: 네, 안녕히 계세요.
A: Goodbye (go well). / B: Yes, goodbye (stay well).
the stayer says 가세요, the leaver answers 계세요 — the reply is the mirror phrase
(손님을 배웅하며) 안녕히 가세요. 또 오세요.
(seeing a customer off) Goodbye. Come again.
everyday: shop staff pair it with 또 오세요 as a warm send-off
(엘리베이터 앞에서) 부장님, 안녕히 가세요. 내일 뵙겠습니다.
(at the elevator) Goodbye, Director. See you tomorrow.
real situation: junior stays, senior leaves — perfect 가세요 context
nuance: 안녕히 가세요 is the goodbye you say to the person who is LEAVING while you remain — 가다 'to go' + polite command, wishing them 'go in peace'. It is the exact partner of 안녕히 계세요 (계시다 'to stay'): the verb encodes who is physically moving. Register ladder: 잘 가 (반말, friend or junior) → 안녕히 가세요 (polite) → 안녕히 가십시오 (격식체, service/formal). For an added caring tone use 조심히 가세요 / 조심히 들어가세요 ('go safely / get home safely'). The big English-speaker trap is that 'goodbye' is one word in English, so learners fire 안녕히 가세요 at the host they are leaving — telling the host to leave their own house. The rule is simple: whoever physically walks away is the 가다 person.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please go in peace' (안녕히 + 가세요 from 가다 'to go'). Said by the person who STAYS — you are sending the departing person off with a warm wish.

Use only when THEY are leaving and you remain. Polite to any adult. Use 안녕히 가십시오 in formal or service settings; drop to 잘 가 with close friends or juniors. Adding 조심히 들어가세요 makes it feel warmer and more caring.
Identical structure, opposite verb: 가세요 (they leave, I stay) vs 계세요 (I leave, they stay). Getting this wrong reverses the meaning entirely. Decide: who is walking? Their verb is 가다.
잘 가 (반말) → 안녕히 가세요 (polite) → 안녕히 가십시오 (격식체). Softer caring variants: 조심히 가세요, 조심히 들어가세요, 안전히 가세요 (all mean 'go safely').

English 'goodbye' is direction-neutral. Korean forces a verb choice. Learners often say 안녕히 가세요 as they themselves walk out — which orders the person staying to 'go away'. Always anchor to: am I leaving (계세요) or are they (가세요)?

mistakes: Saying 안녕히 가세요 when YOU are the one leaving — it orders the person staying to 'go'; if you leave, use 안녕히 계세요.
Using one phrase for everyone like English 'bye' — Korean forces 가세요 (they go) vs 계세요 (you go) based on who actually departs.
Writing 안녕이 가세요 — the adverb is 안녕히 (with 히), never 안녕이.

english: Nice to meet you (for the first time). / How do you do.
usage: 격식 존댓말; first introduction to an adult, esp. someone senior
NOT used; 보다 is too plain — the honorific 뵙다 is required here
I think this is the first time we've met
How do you do, I'm Kim Minsu
natural extension straight into your name
examples: A: 처음 뵙겠습니다. / B: 네, 처음 뵙겠습니다.
A: How do you do. / B: Yes, how do you do.
exchanged mutually at a first meeting — the same phrase bounces back naturally
안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
Hello, nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.
everyday: the standard 3-part first-meeting set — greeting + 처음 뵙겠습니다 + 잘 부탁드립니다
(소개팅/거래처 첫 미팅에서 일어서서 인사하며) 처음 뵙겠습니다. 말씀 많이 들었습니다.
(standing to greet at a blind date / first business meeting) How do you do. I've heard a lot about you.
real situation: pairs with 말씀 많이 들었습니다 — a warm, humble complement to the formal opener
nuance: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the formal phrase for a FIRST meeting — 처음 'first time' + 뵙겠습니다, where 뵙다 is the humble-honorific form of 보다 'to see/meet'. The 겠 adds a polite intentional nuance: 'I will be meeting you for the first time (now)'. You use it toward adults you owe respect: seniors, business contacts, a partner's family. Because 뵙다 is already deeply humble, this phrase has no 반말 version — with a friend-of-a-friend your own age you'd just say 만나서 반가워요. The standard three-piece business self-intro is: 안녕하세요 → 처음 뵙겠습니다 → 잘 부탁드립니다. The English-speaker mistakes are (1) reaching for plain 보다 (처음 보겠습니다), which sounds blunt or rude, and (2) using 만나서 반갑습니다 alone in a stiff formal setting where 처음 뵙겠습니다 is expected first.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '(I) will humbly see you for the first time' — 처음 'first time' + 뵙다 (humble-honorific of 보다 'to see') + 겠습니다 (polite intention). Used as the formal equivalent of 'how do you do / nice to meet you'.

격식 존댓말, exclusively for a FIRST introduction to an adult — especially someone senior, a boss's boss, business contacts, or a partner's family. Once you've met, stop using it (또 뵙겠습니다 / 안녕하세요 for re-meetings). No 반말 equivalent — with casual peers just say 만나서 반가워요.

처음 뵙겠습니다 marks the novelty of the encounter ('it's the first time'). 만나서 반갑습니다 expresses the feeling ('I'm glad to meet you') and can also be used at re-meetings. In formal Korean introductions, lead with 처음 뵙겠습니다, then follow with 만나서 반갑습니다 or 잘 부탁드립니다.
처음 뵙겠습니다 (격식) — no 반말 version. Softer formal: 처음 뵙는 것 같아요. Common full sequence: 처음 뵙겠습니다, [name]라고 합니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
Two errors: (1) Using plain 보다 → 처음 보겠습니다, which drops the required humility and sounds blunt. (2) Relying only on 만나서 반갑습니다 in a stiff formal setting — Koreans expect 처음 뵙겠습니다 there.

mistakes: Saying 처음 보겠습니다 with plain 보다 — it drops the required humility; the honorific 뵙다 → 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the only natural form here.
Using 처음 뵙겠습니다 at a SECOND meeting — it explicitly means 'first time'; once you've met, say 또 뵙겠습니다 or 안녕하세요.
Pronouncing/writing it 처음 봽겠습니다 — the stem is 뵙- (뵙겠습니다), and the verb 뵙다 only fits first/honorific meetings.

english: Nice to meet you. / Glad to meet you.
usage: 격식 존댓말; introductions at work or with seniors
반말, meeting a friend-of-a-friend your own age or younger
해요체; friendly polite, peers and casual acquaintances
I'm glad to have the chance to meet you
examples: A: 만나서 반갑습니다. / B: 저도 반갑습니다.
A: Nice to meet you. / B: Nice to meet you too.
the standard reply is 저도 반갑습니다 ('me too') — not repeating the full sentence
민수 씨 친구분이시죠? 만나서 반가워요.
You're Minsu's friend, right? Nice to meet you.
everyday: 해요체 to a peer you've just been introduced to — warm but not stiff
(명함을 건네며) 안녕하세요, 영업팀 김민수입니다. 만나서 반갑습니다.
(handing over a business card) Hello, I'm Kim Minsu from sales. Nice to meet you.
real situation: business card exchange — 반갑습니다 after 처음 뵙겠습니다 in a full formal intro
nuance: 만나서 반갑습니다 means 'I'm glad to meet you' — 만나서 'having met' + 반갑다 'to be glad'. Unlike 처음 뵙겠습니다, it focuses on the warm feeling of the encounter, not the fact that it's a first meeting, so it can also be used when seeing someone again after a while. Choose the ending by closeness: 반갑습니다 (격식, business/senior) → 반가워요 (polite peers) → 반가워 (반말). Toward an important senior, upgrade the whole phrase: 만나 뵙게 되어 반갑습니다 with the honorific 뵙다. In a formal Korean introduction the sequence is typically: 처음 뵙겠습니다 → 만나서 반갑습니다 → 잘 부탁드립니다. The common English-speaker error is using only 만나서 반갑습니다 for every first meeting and skipping the more formal 처음 뵙겠습니다 opener; also note the reply 저도 반갑습니다, not an echo of the full sentence.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'having met (you), I am glad' — 만나서 (gerund of 만나다 'to meet') + 반갑다 'to be glad'. The focus is the emotional reaction to meeting, not the novelty, so it fits both first meetings and happy reunions.

Works for both first meetings and re-meetings. Choose the ending by relationship: 반갑습니다 (격식, business/seniors) → 반가워요 (polite, casual acquaintances) → 반가워 (반말, friends and juniors). Toward an important VIP or senior elder, upgrade to 만나 뵙게 되어 반갑습니다.

처음 뵙겠습니다 = exclusively 'first time meeting', formal and humble. 만나서 반갑습니다 = 'glad to meet/see you', works on first AND re-meetings, and is more emotionally expressive. In a formal intro, lead with 처음 뵙겠습니다 and follow with 만나서 반갑습니다.
만나서 반가워 (반말) → 만나서 반가워요 (해요체) → 만나서 반갑습니다 (격식) → 만나 뵙게 되어 반갑습니다 (extra-honorific). Reply: 저도 반갑습니다.
Two errors: (1) Using this as the only first-meeting phrase in formal settings — 처음 뵙겠습니다 should come first. (2) Replying with the full sentence again instead of the short 저도 반갑습니다 echo.

mistakes: Saying 만나서 반가워 (반말) to a boss or senior — too casual; use 만나서 반갑습니다 in respectful/formal settings.
Treating it as identical to 처음 뵙겠습니다 — 반갑습니다 = 'glad to meet you' (works for re-meetings too), while 처음 뵙겠습니다 specifically marks a FIRST meeting.
Replying with the whole sentence again instead of 저도 반갑습니다 — Korean prefers the short 'me too' echo.

english: I look forward to working with you. / Please treat me kindly. (lit. I ask for your favor.)
usage: I kindly ask for your favor
격식 존댓말; deeply humble, to seniors/clients/new colleagues
take care of me / look out for me
반말, to a close friend or junior
해요체; polite but a touch softer than 드립니다
I'll be relying on you going forward
examples: A: 잘 부탁드립니다. / B: 네, 저야말로 잘 부탁드립니다.
A: I look forward to working with you. / B: The pleasure is mine.
reply 저야말로 ('it's I who should say so') — standard reciprocal response
오늘부터 함께 일하게 됐습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
I'll be working with you starting today. Please treat me kindly.
everyday: a new hire greeting the team on day one
(결혼 상견례에서 고개 숙이며) 부족한 사람이지만 잘 부탁드립니다.
(bowing at the families' first meeting) I'm not much, but I humbly ask for your kindness.
real situation: in-laws meeting — pairs with a bow and 부족한 사람이지만 ('although I am lacking') to show deep humility
nuance: 잘 부탁드립니다 has no clean English equivalent — literally 'I ask (you) for your favor well', it is a humble set phrase that opens a new relationship: a new job, a class, a project, a partnership, marrying into a family. 부탁드리다 is the humble-honorific 'request' form (부탁하다 → 부탁드리다), so it lowers the speaker and elevates the listener. Register ladder: 잘 부탁해 (반말, friends/juniors) → 잘 부탁드려요 (softer polite) → 잘 부탁드립니다 (격식, seniors/clients). The full formal extension is 앞으로 잘 부탁드리겠습니다. The standard reply is 저야말로 잘 부탁드립니다. There is no real English sentence to translate from, which is exactly the trap: learners either skip it entirely — sounding cold at Korean introductions — or misread it as a concrete 'request', missing that it is purely a relationship-opening courtesy.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I humbly ask for your favorable treatment' (잘 'well/kindly' + 부탁드리다 'to humbly request'). There is no English sentence-for-sentence equivalent; the function is relational, not transactional — it acknowledges that you are entering a relationship where you will depend on the other person.

Said when entering ANY new relationship or role: first day at work, start of a class, client kickoff meeting, a partner's family meeting. Always directed at someone above, beside, or entrusting you — never downward in isolation. Bowing while saying it is expected in formal contexts.

처음 뵙겠습니다 marks it's the first time meeting; 잘 부탁드립니다 asks for ongoing goodwill. They almost always appear together in the sequence: 처음 뵙겠습니다 → 잘 부탁드립니다. 수고하세요 is a parting wish for effort — different context entirely.
잘 부탁해 (반말) → 잘 부탁드려요 (해요체) → 잘 부탁드립니다 (격식) → 앞으로 잘 부탁드리겠습니다 (fullest formal). Reply: 저야말로 잘 부탁드립니다.

English has no equivalent ritual, so learners either skip it (seeming cold or arrogant) or interpret it as a specific request and respond with 'sure, what do you need?' In Korean it is a social formula — the only correct reply is 저야말로 잘 부탁드립니다.

mistakes: Skipping it at a first work/business meeting because it 'has no English' — Koreans expect it; omitting it can read as cold or arrogant.
Using 부탁해 (반말) with a client or senior — far too casual; the humble 잘 부탁드립니다 is required upward.
Writing 잘 부탁드립니다 as 잘 부탁드립니당/부탁드림니다 — the formal ending is 드립니다 (ㅂ니다), not 드림니다.

usage: polite, soft way to ask an adult's name
반말, to a child or close peer/junior
more formal; 성함 is the honorific word for 'name'
natural: offer your own name back
examples: A: 이름이 어떻게 되세요? / B: 김민수예요.
A: What's your name? / B: I'm Kim Minsu.
soft polite name question — 어떻게 되세요? is gentler than 뭐예요?
(첫 수업에서) 학생, 이름이 어떻게 되세요?
(first class) What's your name?
everyday: a teacher asking a new student politely — the same frame works for a colleague you just met
(전화 접수에서) 네, 예약 도와드릴게요. 성함이 어떻게 되세요?
(phone reception) Sure, I'll help with your booking. May I have your name?
real situation: service staff swap 이름 → 성함 to honor the customer — never use 성함 about yourself
nuance: 이름이 어떻게 되세요? literally asks 'how does your name come to be?', but that is simply the standard Korean way to ask for personal info (name, age, job, number) without the bluntness of a direct 뭐예요? For a customer or senior, swap 이름 → 성함: 성함이 어떻게 되세요? is the honorific upgrade. Drop to 반말 이름이 뭐야? only with children or close juniors. A key rule about 성함: it is an honorific noun for the LISTENER, so you must never use it about yourself — answer with plain 이름 (제 이름은 …). The 어떻게 되세요? frame is broadly productive: 나이가 어떻게 되세요? (age), 연락처가 어떻게 되세요? (contact). The English-speaker mistakes are using blunt 이름이 뭐예요? with an adult (childish), and applying the honorific 성함 to yourself ('제 성함은…'), which is grammatically inverted.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'how does your name come to be?' — the 어떻게 되세요 frame is Korean's softened, indirect way of requesting personal information. It does not mean anything unusual; it simply smooths over the directness of a bare '뭐야?' question.

Use 이름이 어떻게 되세요? with any adult you have a polite relationship with. Upgrade to 성함이 어떻게 되세요? for customers, elders, or in service/official contexts. Drop to 이름이 뭐야? only with children or close juniors. The 어떻게 되세요? frame is reusable: swap in 나이, 연락처, 직업 for other polite info questions.

이름 is the neutral word for 'name' — used freely about anyone including yourself. 성함 is the honorific form for the LISTENER's name; you cannot use it about your own name. Service staff and juniors use 성함이 어떻게 되세요?; you reply with 제 이름은 … (not 제 성함은…).
이름이 뭐야? (반말) → 이름이 어떻게 되세요? (polite) → 성함이 어떻게 되세요? (honorific). The frame extends: 나이가 어떻게 되세요? / 연락처가 어떻게 되세요?

Two errors: (1) Asking an adult 이름이 뭐예요? — grammatically okay but blunt and child-directed; 어떻게 되세요? is the adult norm. (2) Saying 제 성함은 … when introducing yourself — 성함 is only for the listener; say 제 이름은 ….

mistakes: Asking an adult 이름이 뭐예요? — understandable but blunt/childish; the courteous form is 이름이 어떻게 되세요? (or 성함이…).
Using 성함 for your OWN name ('제 성함은…') — 성함 is honorific for the listener; about yourself say 제 이름은… .
Saying 이름은 어떻게 되세요? with 은 — the natural particle here is the subject 이/가: 이름이 어떻게 되세요?

english: Where are you from? / Where did you come from?
usage: honorific 오시다; asking an adult their origin
반말, to a peer or junior
natural variant when asking a foreigner's country
examples: A: 어디에서 오셨어요? / B: 미국에서 왔어요.
A: Where are you from? / B: I'm from the US.
answer with [place]에서 왔어요 — 에서 marks origin, not destination
한국말 잘하시네요! 어디에서 오셨어요?
Your Korean is great! Where are you from?
everyday: a very common follow-up compliment + origin question to a foreigner
(모임에서 자기소개 중) 저는 부산에서 왔어요. 혹시 어디에서 오셨어요?
(self-intro at a gathering) I'm from Busan. Where are you from, by the way?
real situation: trading hometowns at a meeting — share yours first, then ask back with 혹시 ('by any chance') to soften it
nuance: 어디에서 오셨어요? asks 'where did you come from?' and works for both home country and hometown — the past tense 오셨- is idiomatic even though origin is ongoing (Korean frames origin as 'where did you set out from'). 오시다 is the honorific of 오다 'to come', so the 시 is non-optional when you owe respect to the listener. The key particle is 에서 ('from'), not 에 ('to/at') — using the wrong one produces 어디에 오셨어요? which asks where they arrived, not where they came from. Register ladder: 어디에서 왔어? (반말) → 어디에서 왔어요? (polite, no honorific) → 어디에서 오셨어요? (honorific) → 어디에서 오셨습니까? (격식체). For a foreigner, 어느 나라에서 오셨어요? is more precise than the open 어디에서. Answers use 에서: 영국에서 왔어요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'where did you (honorably) come from?' — o셨- is honorific past tense of 오다 'to come'. Korean frames origin as 'where did you set out from', which is why past tense fits even for permanent origins.

A natural get-to-know-you question for any context. Use the honorific 시 (오셨어요) with seniors or anyone you owe respect. Drop to 어디에서 왔어? with peers/juniors. For a foreigner where country is the obvious question, 어느 나라에서 오셨어요? is cleaner. Always use 에서 in the answer: 미국에서 왔어요.

에서 = 'from' (origin). 에 = 'to/at' (destination). 어디에서 오셨어요? = 'where are you from?' (correct). 어디에 오셨어요? = 'where did you come to?' (a different question). This particle swap is the most common mistake.
어디에서 왔어? (반말) → 어디에서 왔어요? (no honorific, polite) → 어디에서 오셨어요? (honorific) → 어디에서 오셨습니까? (격식체). Country variant: 어느 나라에서 오셨어요?
Two errors: (1) Using 에 instead of 에서 — 에 is destination, not origin. (2) Dropping the honorific 시 when talking to a senior: 어디에서 왔어요? is polite but lacks the respect that 오셨어요? carries.

mistakes: Saying 어디에 오셨어요? with 에 — 에 = destination ('to where'); origin needs 에서 → 어디에서 오셨어요?
Dropping the honorific and asking an elder 어디에서 왔어요? — to show respect keep 시: 어디에서 오셨어요?
Answering with 에 ('미국에 왔어요') — to state origin use 에서: 미국에서 왔어요.

usage: the everyday polite way to ask someone's job
반말, to a peer or junior
what kind of work do you do?
examples: A: 무슨 일 하세요? / B: 회사 다녀요.
A: What do you do? / B: I work at a company.
common natural answer — 회사 다니다 ('to attend a company') is the everyday way to say 'I work in an office'
아, 그러시군요. 무슨 일 하세요?
Oh, I see. What do you do for work?
everyday: follows small talk naturally — soften sensitive situations with 실례지만 ('if you don't mind')
(소개팅에서) 실례지만 무슨 일 하세요? — 저는 간호사예요.
(on a blind date) May I ask what you do? — I'm a nurse.
real situation: 실례지만 softens the job question, which can feel personal — the 하세요 already carries honorific 시
nuance: 무슨 일 하세요? literally 'what work do you do?' is the natural, polite way to ask someone's job in everyday Korean — Koreans rarely use the textbook 직업이 뭐예요? because it sounds like you're filling out a form. 하세요 already carries the honorific 시, so you get politeness automatically; drop to 반말 무슨 일 해? with peers or juniors, or upgrade to formal 직업이 어떻게 되세요?. Since job questions can feel personal, Koreans often soften them with 실례지만 'excuse me, but…'. A critical confusion for English speakers: 무슨 일 있어요? looks similar but means 'is something the matter? / what's going on?', a completely different function. In this phrase, 일 means 'work/job' and pairs with 하다, not 있다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'what work do you do?' (무슨 'what kind of' + 일 'work/job' + 하세요 'do you do'). In practice this is the normal conversational job question — not formal, not blunt. 일 here means 'job/occupation', not 'a matter/situation'.

Natural get-to-know-you question in casual and semi-formal settings. The honorific 시 in 하세요 is built in, making it automatically polite. Add 실례지만 before it when you want to be extra tactful. Avoid the even blunter 직업이 뭐예요? unless filling out a form.

무슨 일 하세요? = 'what do you do for work?' (occupation). 무슨 일 있어요? = 'is something the matter? / what's going on?' (a completely different sentence). The difference is 하다 (do work) vs 있다 (there is / something exists). Do not confuse them.
무슨 일 해? (반말) → 무슨 일 하세요? (polite) → 어떤 일 하세요? (softer, 'what kind') → 직업이 어떻게 되세요? (formal). Softener: 실례지만 무슨 일 하세요?

Two errors: (1) Over-relying on stiff 직업이 뭐예요? in casual talk — it sounds like a survey question. (2) Confusing 무슨 일 하세요? (job) with 무슨 일 있어요? (something wrong?) — one swaps 하다 for 있다 but the meaning flips entirely.

mistakes: Defaulting to 직업이 뭐예요? in casual talk — grammatically fine but textbook-stiff; Koreans say 무슨 일 하세요?
Confusing it with 무슨 일 있어요? — that asks 'is something the matter?'; for someone's job it's 무슨 일 하세요?
Dropping 시 with a senior (무슨 일 해요?) — keep the honorific: 무슨 일 하세요?

english: Long time no see. / It's been a while.
usage: 해요체; to someone you know but aren't super close with
격식체; to a senior, client, or in a formal setting
it's really been ages, have you been well?
natural extension into 'how have you been?'
examples: A: 오랜만이에요! / B: 그러게요, 정말 오랜만이에요.
A: Long time no see! / B: Right, it really has been a while.
agree with 그러게요 ('I know, right') + repeat — the warmest natural response
어, 민수 씨! 오랜만이에요. 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요?
Oh, Minsu! Long time no see. How have you been all this time?
everyday: 오랜만이에요 pairs seamlessly with 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요? ('how've you been since then?')
(동창회에서) 야, 진짜 오랜만이다! 너 하나도 안 변했네.
(at a reunion) Wow, it's been SO long! You haven't changed at all.
real situation: 반말 오랜만이다 among old friends — 이야 / 이다 endings are casual exclamatory forms
nuance: 오랜만이에요 means 'it's been a long time' and is the warm opener when reuniting with someone you haven't seen in a while — 오랜만 is a contracted form of 오래간만 ('after a long interval'). The ending determines register: 오랜만이야/이다 (반말, close friends) → 오랜만이에요 (polite, acquaintances) → 오랜만입니다 (격식, seniors/clients). Note the copula: 오랜만 ends in a consonant (ㄴ), so the 해요체 ending is -이에요, not -예요. It naturally chains into 잘 지냈어요? or 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요?. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, the spelling — it's 오랜만 (from 오래간만, not 오랫만, a very common native typo); second, translating 'long time no see' word-for-word as 오래 안 봤어요, which is understandable but not the natural set phrase.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it is a long interval' — 오랜만 from 오래간만 'after a long while' + -이에요 copula (이에요 because 오랜만 ends in a consonant). Used as the warm reunion opener 'long time no see'.

Only use when a genuine gap has passed — days at minimum, usually weeks or months. Do not use it with someone you saw recently. Say it the moment you spot them, before 안녕하세요 or right after. Chain it into 잘 지냈어요? / 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요? for a fuller greeting.

오래 안 봤어요 ('I haven't seen you for a long time') is the descriptive sentence; 오랜만이에요 is the fixed idiomatic greeting. Use 오랜만이에요 as the set opener — it sounds more natural and native than the descriptive form.
오랜만이야/이다 (반말) → 오랜만이에요 (해요체) → 오랜만입니다 (격식체). Intensity: 정말 오랜만이에요 / 너무 오랜만이에요 / 오랜만이다, 진짜!

Two mistakes: (1) Spelling it 오랫만이에요 — the correct form is 오랜만 (from 오래간만), not 오랫만. (2) Translating 'long time no see' literally as 오래 안 봤어요 — understandable, but the natural fixed greeting is 오랜만이에요.

mistakes: Writing 오랫만이에요 — the correct spelling is 오랜만이에요 (from 오래간만); 오랫만 is wrong.
Saying 오래 안 봤어요 to mean 'long time no see' — understandable but unnatural; the set greeting is 오랜만이에요.
Using 오랜만이에요 with someone you saw yesterday — it implies a genuinely long gap; for a short break just say 안녕하세요.

english: Have you been well? / How have you been?
usage: 해요체; greeting someone you haven't seen in a while
adds honorific 시, toward a senior
been well? nothing's come up, right?
examples: A: 잘 지냈어요? / B: 네, 잘 지냈어요. OO 씨는요?
A: Have you been well? / B: Yes, I've been well. And you?
echo the same phrase and bounce it back with 씨는요? — this is the expected rhythm
오랜만이에요! 그동안 잘 지냈어요?
Long time no see! Have you been well all this time?
everyday: follows 오랜만이에요 naturally — 그동안 'all this time/meanwhile' connects the gap
(문자로) 선배님, 잘 지내셨어요? 오랜만에 연락드려요.
(by text) Have you been well, senior? It's been a while since I reached out.
real situation: reconnecting text to a senior — honorific 지내셨어요, and 연락드려요 ('I'm reaching out') adds humility
nuance: 잘 지냈어요? literally 'did you spend (time) well?' is the reunion 'how have you been?' — past tense because it asks about the specific stretch of time since you last met. That past-tense focus is what makes it pair naturally with 오랜만이에요; asking 잘 지냈어요? to someone you see every day sounds strangely probing, as though something might have happened. For an ongoing current-state question, use present-tense 잘 지내요? or 어떻게 지내세요?. Register ladder: 잘 지냈어? (반말) → 잘 지냈어요? (polite) → 잘 지내셨어요? (honorific, to seniors). The English-speaker trap is mapping it onto the rote English 'how are you?' and firing it at strangers or casual daily encounters — in Korean it genuinely implies real time has passed and that you care about the answer.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'did you spend (the time) well?' — 잘 'well' + 지냈어요 past tense of 지내다 'to live/get by'. The past tense anchors it to the gap since your last meeting, making it the 'how have you been?' of reunions, not a daily check-in.

Use only when a real gap has passed since you last saw or spoke with this person — it pairs naturally with 오랜만이에요. Do NOT use with someone you encounter daily (a daily coworker, a neighbor you see every morning); it implies distance. With seniors add 시: 잘 지내셨어요?

잘 지냈어요? is past tense — 'how were things since we last met?' 어떻게 지내세요? is present tense — 'how are things going now/these days?' After a reunion, 잘 지냈어요? is the right opener; for checking on someone's current life, 어떻게 지내세요? fits.
잘 지냈어? (반말) → 잘 지냈어요? (polite) → 잘 지내셨어요? (honorific). Extensions: 잘 지냈어요? 별일 없었죠? / 그동안 잘 지냈어요?

English 'how are you?' is a daily pleasantry with no expected real answer. Korean 잘 지냈어요? genuinely implies time has passed and invites a real reply. Using it daily or with strangers sounds as if you suspect something happened to them — reserve it for actual reunions.

mistakes: Using 잘 지냈어요? as a casual 'how are you?' to a stranger — it implies you've not met for a while; greet new/everyday people with 안녕하세요.
Dropping 시 with a senior (잘 지냈어요?) when more respect is wanted — use 잘 지내셨어요?.
Confusing past 지냈어요? (since we last met) with present 지내요? (these days) — pick the tense to match your meaning.

english: How are you doing (these days)? / How's it going?
usage: honorific 지내시다; to someone you know, present state
격식체; formal or to a senior/official
how have you been doing lately?
examples: A: 어떻게 지내세요? / B: 그냥 그래요.
A: How are you doing? / B: So-so.
a real, honest answer — 그냥 그래요 ('just so-so') is genuinely common and not rude
오랜만이에요. 요즘 어떻게 지내세요?
Long time no see. How have you been lately?
everyday: 오랜만이에요 + 요즘 어떻게 지내세요? — a warm reunion opener that invites a real update
(통화에서) 어머니, 요즘 어떻게 지내세요? 건강은 괜찮으시고요?
(on the phone) Mom, how have you been lately? Is your health okay?
real situation: honorific check-in with a parent — 세요 is appropriate even with close family when showing respect
nuance: 어떻게 지내세요? asks 'how are you getting on these days?' about someone's present life — 지내다 'to live/get by' + honorific 시 + present tense. Unlike 잘 지냈어요? (past, 'since we last met'), this is about the NOW and is a genuine open question, not a social placeholder. Adding 요즘 'lately' makes it even more natural. Register ladder: 어떻게 지내? (반말) → 어떻게 지내세요? (polite) → 어떻게 지내십니까? (격식체). The key English-speaker mistake is treating it like the rote English 'how are you?' that expects only 'fine, thanks' — Korean acquaintances asking this genuinely want an answer (잘 지내요 / 그냥 그래요 / 바빠요). Also, never open with this to a brand-new stranger — lead with 안녕하세요 first; 어떻게 지내세요? assumes prior acquaintance.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'how are you getting by?' (어떻게 'how' + 지내세요 honorific present of 지내다 'to live/get by'). Present tense — unlike 잘 지냈어요? (past), this asks about ongoing life right now.

Use with someone you have prior acquaintance with. It implies you know something about their life and are genuinely checking in. Requires 시 (→ 지내세요) when addressing a senior. Adding 요즘 'these days' makes it feel more specific and warm. Do NOT fire at strangers — 안녕하세요 comes first.

어떻게 지내세요? = present, about current life now. 잘 지냈어요? = past, about the gap since the last meeting. Both are reunion-type questions, but 어떻게 지내세요? can also be used in ongoing relationships ('checking in on you lately'), while 잘 지냈어요? only fits after a real gap.
어떻게 지내? (반말) → 어떻게 지내요? (no honorific, casual polite) → 어떻게 지내세요? (honorific 시) → 어떻게 지내십니까? (격식). Extend: 요즘 어떻게 지내세요? / 요즘 어떻게 지내고 있어요?

English 'how are you?' expects 'fine thanks' — no real answer. Korean 어떻게 지내세요? genuinely invites one. Giving a one-word 'fine' and pivoting can feel cold. Equally, opening with this phrase to someone you just met (instead of 안녕하세요) sounds presumptuous.

mistakes: Using it as a meaningless 'how are you?' to a stranger — it invites a real answer and implies acquaintance; greet new people with 안녕하세요.
Mixing it up with 잘 지냈어요? — 어떻게 지내세요? = now/these days; 잘 지냈어요? = the period since you last met.
Dropping 시 with someone you respect (어떻게 지내요?) — keep the honorific: 어떻게 지내세요?.

english: See you again. / See you later.
usage: 해요체; warm, friendly parting with someone you'll see again
격식체; honorific 뵙다, to a senior/client
examples: A: 그럼 또 봬요! / B: 네, 또 봬요.
A: See you again then! / B: Yes, see you.
a light, friendly mutual close — the phrase is fully interchangeable as greeting and reply
오늘 즐거웠어요. 다음에 또 봬요.
I had a good time today. See you again next time.
everyday: after a pleasant meetup — 다음에 ('next time') makes the plan explicit
(거래처를 나서며) 오늘 시간 내주셔서 감사합니다. 또 뵙겠습니다.
(leaving a client) Thank you for your time today. I'll see you again.
real situation: business context — upgrade to formal 또 뵙겠습니다 with the honorific 뵙다
nuance: 또 봬요 means 'let's see each other again' — 또 'again' + 봬요, the contracted polite form of 뵈어요 (from honorific 뵈다 'to see someone you respect'). It is a warm, optimistic parting that implies you genuinely expect to meet again, softer than a bare 안녕히 가세요. Register ladder: 또 봐 (반말) → 또 봬요 (polite) → 또 뵙겠습니다 (격식, to seniors/clients). The spelling is one of Korean's notorious traps even for natives: it's 봬요, NOT 뵈요 — the test: 뵈 + 어요 contracts to 봬요 (like 되 + 어요 → 돼요). Learners also reach for 나중에 봐요 as a 'see you later' translation, but 또 봬요 / 다음에 봬요 sound more natural as set partings. Never confuse 봬요 (see/meet, from 뵈다) with 봐요 (look at, from 보다).

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'again I will see (you humbly)' — 또 'again' + 봬요 contracted from 뵈어요 (honorific 뵈다 'to see someone respected'). Used as the warm 'see you next time / see you around'.

A warm friendly parting implying mutual expectation to meet again. Use with any polite acquaintance. Upgrade to 또 뵙겠습니다 when speaking to a senior, boss, or business client. Drop to 또 봐 in 반말 with close friends. Adding 다음에 ('next time') makes the future meeting more concrete.

안녕히 가세요 is a neutral, directional goodbye (stayer to leaver). 또 봬요 is warmer and forward-looking — it expresses you want to see this person again. Use 안녕히 가세요 with strangers; 또 봬요 with acquaintances you're genuinely happy to see again.
또 봐 (반말) → 또 봬요 (해요체) → 또 뵙겠습니다 (격식). Extensions: 다음에 또 봬요 / 곧 또 봬요 ('see you soon'). Intensified: 꼭 또 봬요 ('we must meet again').

The notorious spelling trap: 봬요 (뵈+어요 → 봬요), NOT 뵈요 — the same contraction rule as 되+어요 → 돼요. Also, do NOT confuse with 봐요 (look at something, from 보다). 나중에 봐요 ('see you later', literally) sounds unnatural as a set parting — 또 봬요 is the natural phrase.

mistakes: Writing 또 뵈요 — the correct contraction is 봬요 (뵈어요 → 봬요); 뵈요 is a spelling error.
Confusing 봬요 (see/meet, honorific) with 봐요 (look at, plain 보다) — for parting it's 또 봬요.
Using 또 봬요 with a senior where formality is expected — upgrade to the honorific 또 뵙겠습니다.

english: Take care. / Get home safe. (lit. Please go in[side].)
usage: parting wish that they get home/inside safely; also ends phone calls
get home safe / go on in
반말, to a close friend or junior
격식체; to a senior or customer
examples: A: 그럼 들어가세요. / B: 네, 들어가세요.
A: Take care then. / B: Yes, you too.
exchanged mutually as you part — each says it to the other, wishing both a safe return
늦었네요, 조심히 들어가세요.
It's late — get home safely.
everyday: 조심히 들어가세요 is the warmer, more caring variant — especially natural at night
(통화를 마치며) 네, 알겠습니다. 그럼 들어가세요.
(ending a call) Okay, got it. Take care then.
real situation: 들어가세요 closes phone calls naturally — it is NOT telling you to literally walk indoors
nuance: 들어가세요 literally means 'please go in(side)', but as a farewell it wishes the other person a safe journey home — think of it as 'get home safe / take care'. It also doubles as the standard way to end a phone call ('okay, talk to you later / take care'). Compared to 안녕히 가세요, 들어가세요 feels more caring and intimate; you use it with people you have real warmth toward rather than pure strangers. The caring upgrade 조심히 들어가세요 ('go in carefully') is extremely common and slightly warmer. Register ladder: 들어가 (반말) → 들어가세요 (polite) → 들어가십시오 (격식). The English-speaker confusion is taking 들어가세요 literally — at a doorway it can sound like a command to step inside, and on a phone call it has nothing to do with walking. Context always signals it as a warm farewell.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please go in(side)' — 들어가다 'to go/come in'. The literal image is the other person entering their home, but as a parting phrase it simply means 'take care / get home safe'. On the phone it means 'goodbye, look after yourself'.

Said when you part ways and the other person is heading home or elsewhere. Especially warm at night or after a long meeting. Doubles as a standard phone-call closer. Use 조심히 들어가세요 to add a caring note. Avoid using it with complete strangers you have no warmth toward — 안녕히 가세요 is more neutral there.

안녕히 가세요 is neutral, directional, used even with strangers. 들어가세요 is warmer and more personal — it imagines the person arriving home safely. 조심히 가세요 ('go carefully') is the mid-point: caring but not as domestically specific as 들어가세요.
들어가 (반말) → 들어가세요 (polite) → 들어가십시오 (격식). Caring upgrades: 조심히 들어가세요 / 안전히 들어가세요. Phone closing: 그럼 들어가세요, 다음에 또 연락할게요.

The literal 'go inside' reading misleads learners: at a physical doorway it can seem like a command to step in, and on a phone call it clearly can't mean that. In both cases it is simply a warm farewell — 'take care / get home safely'.

mistakes: Reading 들어가세요 on the phone as literally 'go inside' — at the end of a call it just means 'take care / bye'.
Saying 들어가세요 to someone who is NOT heading home/inside — it wishes a safe trip home; otherwise use 안녕히 가세요.
Using 반말 들어가 with a senior — for respect say 들어가세요 (or 들어가십시오).

usage: polite parting, esp. service staff or daytime goodbyes
반말, to a friend (보내 'spend' avoids the grammar issue)
preferred polite form: '(you) spend a good day'
natural variant; swap 하루 for 주말/저녁
examples: A: 좋은 하루 되세요! / B: 네, 감사합니다.
A: Have a good day! / B: Thanks, you too.
the everyday upbeat sign-off — the reply 감사합니다 or 네, 고마워요 is natural
(카페에서 나가며) 감사합니다, 좋은 하루 되세요.
(leaving a cafe) Thank you, have a good day.
everyday: customer ↔ staff exchange — service staff say it constantly throughout the day
(금요일 퇴근하며) 다들 고생하셨어요. 좋은 주말 되세요!
(leaving work Friday) Good work everyone. Have a good weekend!
real situation: swap in 좋은 주말 되세요 on a Friday — 다들 ('everyone') makes it a group send-off
nuance: 좋은 하루 되세요 is the cheerful 'have a good day' you hear constantly from shop and cafe staff; it works as a warm daytime goodbye to anyone. The noun can be swapped: 좋은 주말 되세요 (Friday/weekend), 좋은 저녁 되세요 (evening), 좋은 하루 보내세요 (cleaner grammar). The 되다 vs 보내다 grammar debate: strictly, 되다 means 'become', so 좋은 하루 되세요 reads as 'please become a good day', which is grammatically awkward — careful or formal Korean prefers 좋은 하루 보내세요 ('spend a good day'). In practice, 되세요 is everywhere and fully accepted, but writing 보내세요 in a formal context is safer. For 반말 with friends, 좋은 하루 보내 is the cleanest form. The English-speaker pitfall is using 되세요 as the all-day-all-situation default, when at night 좋은 저녁 되세요 is more fitting, and for a general parting 안녕히 가세요 or 들어가세요 is more natural.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please become a good day' (좋은 하루 + 되세요 from 되다 'to become'). The 'become' reading is odd, which is why 좋은 하루 보내세요 ('spend a good day') is considered the grammatically correct form. In everyday speech, 되세요 is fully natural.

A cheerful daytime parting, especially in service contexts. Use with any polite acquaintance when saying goodbye during the day. Swap 하루 for 주말 on Fridays, 저녁 in the evening, 한 주 at the start/end of a week. Not natural as a nighttime farewell — use 들어가세요 or 안녕히 가세요 then.

좋은 하루 되세요 (되다 'to become') is the ubiquitous informal form heard everywhere. 좋은 하루 보내세요 (보내다 'to spend/send') is the grammatically tighter form preferred in writing and formal contexts. Both are correct in daily speech; 보내세요 sounds slightly more educated.
좋은 하루 보내 (반말) → 좋은 하루 보내세요 (formal polite) / 좋은 하루 되세요 (casual polite). Noun swaps: 좋은 주말 되세요 / 좋은 저녁 되세요 / 좋은 한 주 보내세요.

English 'have a nice day' works at any time of day. Korean 하루 specifically means 'day' — saying it at night is slightly odd. Also, overusing it for every goodbye instead of 들어가세요 or 안녕히 가세요 can sound formulaic or customer-service-ish.

mistakes: Using 좋은 하루 되세요 at night — for evening say 좋은 저녁 되세요; 하루 fits the daytime.
Writing the 반말 as 좋은 하루 돼 — for friends use 좋은 하루 보내; 보내다 sidesteps the 되다 awkwardness.
Treating 되세요 as the 'most correct' — careful/formal Korean prefers 좋은 하루 보내세요 ('spend a good day').

usage: 격식체; opening a self-intro to a group or in a formal setting
examples: A: 자, 신입사원분 소개를 부탁드릴게요. / B: 네, 제 소개를 하겠습니다. 이번에 입사한 김민수입니다.
A: Now, please go ahead and introduce yourself, new employee. / B: Of course. Let me introduce myself — I'm Kim Minsu, newly joined.
A/B exchange: host invites the intro and the speaker opens formally with 제 소개를 하겠습니다 before giving their name
안녕하세요, 제 소개를 할게요. 저는 부산에서 온 민수예요.
Hello, let me introduce myself. I'm Minsu from Busan.
everyday: 해요체 intro at a small gathering or first meeting with peers
(첫 출근 회의에서 일어서며) 안녕하세요, 간단히 제 소개를 하겠습니다. 이번에 입사한 김민수입니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
(standing at a first-day meeting) Hello, let me briefly introduce myself. I'm Kim Minsu, newly joined. I look forward to working with you.
real situation: the complete formal intro sequence — 간단히 ('briefly') signals you won't overrun, then name + role + 잘 부탁드립니다
nuance: 제 소개를 하겠습니다 is the set opener for introducing yourself to a group — 제 'my (humble)' + 소개 'introduction' + 하겠습니다, where 겠 signals polite intention ('I will now do'). 제 is the humble first-person possessive (from 저), correctly paired with formal speech; using 내 (from 나) in the same sentence would clash registers. Register ladder: 내 소개를 할게 (반말) → 제 소개를 할게요 (polite) → 제 소개를 하겠습니다 (격식체). Adding 간단히 ('briefly') before it is extremely common and shows consideration for listeners' time. The phrase conventionally bookends with 잘 부탁드립니다 at the end. The English-speaker mistakes are mismatching 내 with a formal ending, and trying to construct a 'myself' reflexive phrase like '저를 소개하겠습니다' — the idiomatic Korean is 제 소개를 하겠습니다, with 소개 as the object.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I will do my (humble) introduction' — 제 (humble 'my') + 소개 'introduction' + 하겠습니다 (polite intentional future). The 겠 signals that the speaker is about to do something now, making it a performative opener.

Used when addressing a group for the first time — a work team, a class, a formal gathering. The speaker stands (in formal settings), often bows slightly, and delivers the intro. For one-on-one introductions, 처음 뵙겠습니다 is more natural; this phrase signals a group audience.

'저를 소개하겠습니다' ('I will introduce me to you') is grammatically possible but rare and clunky for a self-intro. The natural idiom is 제 소개를 하겠습니다 (소개 as object). Also: 자기소개를 하겠습니다 ('I will do a self-introduction') is another formal variant.
내 소개를 할게 (반말) → 제 소개를 할게요 (해요체) → 제 소개를 하겠습니다 (격식). With 간단히: 간단히 제 소개를 하겠습니다. Bookend: … + 잘 부탁드립니다.

Two errors: (1) Saying 내 소개를 하겠습니다 — 내 is 반말 'my'; it clashes with the formal 하겠습니다 ending. Always pair humble 제 with formal endings. (2) Constructing a reflexive 'introduce myself' as 저를 소개하겠습니다 — the natural set phrase uses 소개 as the noun object: 제 소개를 하겠습니다.

mistakes: Saying 내 소개를 하겠습니다 — 내 is 반말 'my'; with formal 하겠습니다 use the humble 제: 제 소개를 하겠습니다.
Using 반말 내 소개를 할게 in a formal/work intro — too casual; use 제 소개를 하겠습니다.
Forgetting to follow with your name + 잘 부탁드립니다 — Korean self-intros conventionally close with 잘 부탁드립니다.

english: Have you eaten? (a common Korean greeting)
usage: 해요체; a warm, caring everyday greeting, not a literal dinner invite
반말, to a close friend, sibling, or junior
honorific 식사하시다; to a senior, in-law, or someone you respect
highest respect; 진지/드시다 are honorific words, for grandparents/elderly
examples: A: 밥 먹었어요? / B: 네, 먹었어요. OO 씨는요?
A: Have you eaten? / B: Yes, I have. And you?
treated as 'how are you?' — answer briefly and bounce it back; no need to describe what you ate
(점심시간쯤 마주쳐서) 어, 안녕하세요. 식사하셨어요?
(running into someone around lunchtime) Oh, hello. Have you eaten?
everyday: 식사하셨어요? is the polite honorific version — natural with coworkers, seniors, or near mealtimes
(엄마가 전화로) 아들, 밥은 먹고 다녀? 끼니 거르지 마.
(Mom on the phone) Son, are you eating properly? Don't skip meals.
real situation: 반말 밥 먹었어? / 밥은 먹고 다녀? as an expression of parental care — the food question = 'I'm worried about you'
nuance: 밥 먹었어요? literally 'did you eat (rice/a meal)?' is one of Korea's most iconic greetings — historically food was scarce, so asking whether someone had eaten was an act of care; today it functions much like English 'how are you?', not as a literal question about food. It is emphatically NOT an invitation to eat together; the expected reply is a quick 네, 먹었어요 or 아직요, and then bounce the question back. Register ladder: 밥 먹었어? (반말) → 밥 먹었어요? (polite) → 식사하셨어요? (honorific, 밥→식사 + 시) → 진지 드셨어요? (for grandparents/elderly, with full honorific nouns 진지/드시다). Use the 식사하셨어요? or 진지 드셨어요? upgrades for anyone you owe deep respect; plain 밥 먹었어요? among peers is warm and casual. The English-speaker mistake is taking the question at face value — either thinking they're being invited to a meal, or starting to describe the full menu they just ate.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'did you eat (rice/a meal)?' (밥 'cooked rice/meal' + 먹었어요 past of 먹다 'to eat'). In modern use it functions as a caring social greeting — the food question carries emotional warmth ('I'm thinking about your well-being'), not a real food-status inquiry.

Natural near mealtimes and as a greeting when you bump into an acquaintance. More caring and intimate than 안녕하세요 — you'd say it to someone you know. Never use 밥 먹었어? (반말) with a senior; use 식사하셨어요? or 진지 드셨어요?. Do NOT interpret it as an invitation to eat.

밥 = neutral 'rice/meal' (everyday speech). 식사 (食事) = Sino-Korean, slightly more formal. 진지 = honorific noun for an elder's meal, paired with 드시다 (honorific of 먹다). The ladder: 밥 먹었어? → 밥 먹었어요? → 식사하셨어요? → 진지 드셨어요?
밥 먹었어? (반말) → 밥 먹었어요? (해요체) → 식사하셨어요? (honorific) → 진지 드셨어요? (elderly). Variants: 식사는 하셨어요? / 밥은 먹었어? (added 은 softens slightly).

Two mistakes: (1) Thinking it is a dinner invitation — it is not; reply 네, 먹었어요 and move on. (2) Giving a detailed answer about your meal ('I had 순두부찌개 and 된장국...') — the ritual reply is one line, then return the question.

mistakes: Taking 밥 먹었어요? literally as a dinner invitation — it's a caring greeting like 'how are you?'; just answer 네, 먹었어요 and ask back.
Using 밥 먹었어? (반말) with a senior — upgrade to 식사하셨어요?, or 진지 드셨어요? for an elderly person.
Answering by describing your whole meal — the ritual reply is short (네, 먹었어요 / 아직 안 먹었어요), then return the question.
